title: PATTERNS: GENERATIONAL CYCLE
mv: When I call to remembrance the genuine faith that is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am persuaded is in you also.
mvp: “When I call to remembrance the genuine faith that is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am persuaded is in you also.” 2Timothy 1:5 (NKJV)
assignment: Identify one negative pattern (such as anger, fear, dishonesty, addiction, or broken relationships) that seems to have repeated itself in your family or community. Use your knowledge in this lesson to break this pattern and establish a new godly legacy for the next generation (No mark).

b.x: A pattern is essentially something that repeats or follows a rule, making it possible to recognise and often predict what comes next. The pattern of generational cycles, recurring behaviours, blessings, struggles, or sins passed from one generation to another, is a significant and recurring theme in the Bible.
Harmful patterns can be categorised under four major patterns:

i: Emotional/behavioural patterns such as anger, rage, addiction, abandonment, fear, anxiety, etc.
Relational/social patterns, e.g. separation, divorce, sexual dysfunction, favouritism, unhealthy rivalry, etc.
Spiritual patterns like hostility towards spiritual things, witchcraft, rebellion against spiritual authority, lukewarmness, unbelief, cynicism, etc.
Financial/occupational patterns which may include poverty, irresponsibility, laziness, workaholic, mismanagement, etc.

b.x: When we study the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, we see that their lives were marked by similar events, character flaws, and experiences. These include: Struggles over wells and land (Genesis 21:25-30; 26:18-22), deception (Genesis 12:13; Genesis 26:7-9), family favouritism and conflict (Genesis 25:28; Genesis 37:3-4), delay in childbearing (Genesis 21:5; Genesis 25:19-21, 26; Genesis 30:1-2, 22-24).

David’s family had a pattern of lust, adultery and conflicts (2 Samuel 11:1-4; 13:10-14; 15:13-14; 1 Kings 11:1-3). Ahab and Jezebel had a family pattern of idolatry, murder and judgement (1 Kings 21:11-16; 2 Kings 11:1-3; 2 Kings 9-10). Eli the Priest had a pattern of ministerial negligence and divine judgement (1 Samuel 2:12-17, 31; 1 Kings 2:27). The line of Cain had a pattern of rebellion and violence (Genesis 4:8, 23-24).

To break free from negative generational patterns, you must recognize the pattern that is prevalent in your lineage, engage in prayer and fasting (Isaiah 49:24-26), repent and renounce it (Daniel 9:4-5; Galatians 3:13-14), renew your mind with the word of God for positive transformation (Romans 12:2), seek wise counsel and accountability partner (Proverbs 11:14), break the cycle (Ezekiel 18:19-20), and establish a new pattern through Christ (2Corinthians 5:17).
God promises to show mercy to a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments (Exodus 20:6).

Positive generational cycles are characterised by faithfulness to God, obedience, and the intentional transmission of godly values from one generation to another. For instance, Abraham's faith and obedience established a covenant with God; this brought blessings for his descendants and created a lasting legacy for the nation of Israel (Genesis 17:5-7). While David was imperfect, his genuine devotion to God created a positive legacy; his faithfulness established a covenant promise for his descendants (2 Samuel 7:8-16). The sincere faith in Timothy's family was a powerful and positive generational influence, signifying the impact of godliness on future generations (2 Timothy 1:5).
God expects that your faith-walk should not end with your generation; you must pass it on to your children, grandchildren, and beyond as a positive generational pattern (Genesis 18:19).

i: What are the steps to breaking negative patterns?
Identify three characteristics of positive generational patterns.
